speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The stability of our financial system lies in sound lending practices, so that financial institutions lend to individuals and corporates who are creditworthy and able to repay their loans over time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Credit bureaus serve the purpose of providing borrowers' information to help financial institutions assess the creditworthiness of their potential clients.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Also, the reliability of the banks' credit rating systems is enhanced by the availability of more complete credit information.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With these objectives in mind, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had in 2001 encouraged the industry to consider establishing a consumer credit bureau to facilitate comprehensive credit risk assessment of their customers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2002, the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS), together with several private sector partners, set up the Credit Bureau (Singapore) Pte Ltd (CBS), Singapore's first consumer credit bureau.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: CBS was recognised by MAS and subjected to confidentiality undertakings to safeguard banking data.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2009, MAS recognised a second credit bureau operated by DP Credit Bureau Pte Ltd (DPCB).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Both credit bureaus collate consumer credit information from MAS-regulated financial institutions, such as banks, finance companies and credit card companies, and share the information with all members to facilitate their credit assessments and loan underwriting decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As credit bureaus collect larger amounts of and more detailed borrower information, it would be prudent to subject them to closer supervision by MAS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The current regulatory regime is inadequate as it only allows MAS to recognise or revoke the recognition of credit bureaus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS does not have any other powers to exercise effective supervision over credit bureaus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, to help ensure that they take adequate measures to safeguard the confidentiality, security and integrity of sensitive borrower information.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, to better ensure the credit bureaus operate soundly in a way that protects consumer interests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill has been modelled after similar regimes in other countries, such as Australia and the US.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, the Bill will empower MAS to license credit bureaus and subject them to corporate governance and operational requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To promote good corporate governance, only fit and proper persons can be appointed to senior management positions in a licensed credit bureau.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In addition, MAS will have powers to approve controlling shareholdings as well as the appointment and removal of directors and chief executives of licensed credit bureaus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Licensed credit bureaus are also required to meet operational standards, which are specified in the Bill and subsidiary legislations, such as Regulations and Notices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These include having robust controls in credit reporting processes, accurate and complete credit data specifications, secure information technology systems, and sound business continuity management, amongst others.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In addition, MAS will be empowered to inspect and investigate licensed credit bureaus and assume control of them, should they come under duress or distress.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, the Bill will empower MAS to require licensed credit bureaus and their approved members to safeguard the confidentiality, security and integrity of customer credit information.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will provide greater assurance that the credit data provided by licensed credit bureaus and used by approved members to process consumer credit applications are accurate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To achieve this, licensed credit bureaus and their approved members will be required to put in place adequate controls to safeguard against data loss and unauthorised access to data.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To help ensure that the credit information is accurate and complete, the Bill will require approved members to submit accurate and complete data to the licensed credit bureau in a timely manner and at regular intervals.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS will have powers to investigate and sanction approved members of licensed credit bureaus for credit reporting breaches.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are existing requirements under the Banking Act to restrict disclosure of confidential customer information to credit bureaus and their members for purposes other than for credit assessment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, the Bill requires licensed credit bureaus and their approved members to protect consumers' rights to access, review and rectify the customer information held by the credit bureaus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Licensed credit bureaus will be required to offer various channels for consumers to access their credit reports.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will facilitate easy access and review of credit records by customers, provide them with a consolidated view of their credit positions and credit standing as viewed by their creditors and allow consumers to dispute any inaccurate or incomplete data.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Where disputes are raised, the Bill requires licensed credit bureaus and their approved members to conduct prompt investigations and rectify the erroneous records in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From education to buying a house and furnishing it, to travelling, it is almost a norm now to go cashless.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With online purchasing and services offering consumers a flexible array of options, having a credit card to make payments safely online is almost a must.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not only are cashless or prepaid transactions more convenient, when used wisely, it can help one to save money.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, instead of spending thousands a year on rental while trying to save up for a dream home, one can quickly own a home by taking out a loan and buying on credit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It also means that more money can be availed for investments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, with so many banks and financial institutions, and a large number of others from travel operators, furniture outlets and so on, offering loans and collecting customer credit information, it is important that a good database is built on each individual who seeks to use the "buy now, pay later" schemes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will help these institutions and others offering delayed payment options to safeguard their interest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also a way for consumers to learn to be prudent in their spending and there are checks in place when a limit is hit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While most people are generally prudent with their expenses, there are some who are callous with their finances and they end up trying to consume more than they can chew.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The result: legal summonses with a view to being made a bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as the data is being collected and collated, we need to ensure that the credit bureaus have safeguards in place to ensure that the individual's personal data are not being compromised.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a welcomed move that will give consumers the assurance that their data would be in safe hands.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope that MAS will pay close attention, especially to the security systems that licensed credit bureaus (LCBs) are using to manage customer information.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And, from the experience of "insiders", these bureaus should also ensure that staff who have access to sensitive information are properly screened before they are employed and, even after employment, they are monitored to avoid the leaks that we see peppering the news in the US.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It should be made mandatory that these institutions review and update their systems periodically in accordance with current trends and developments in technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the main reasons for poor financial management is the lack of access to comprehensive credit reports.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We tend to spend more freely when no physical cash exchanges hands.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Without keeping prudent records, one's spending can easily snowball and spiral out of control.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of them would roll over the debts to the next month.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some would rack up such large debts that they would take out additional loans to pay off the debts, and it then turns into a vicious cycle.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Was there a time lag between the time someone credits a mischief with his multiple credit cards before the data is fed to a bureau monitoring system?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Credit reports are essential to good money management as they help to keep track of credit payment history compiled from different credit providers and, in turn, empowering consumers to manage their spending more responsibly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A comprehensive report will also enable credit providers to make wiser lending decisions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The lack of comprehensive credit details and poor judgement on the part of credit bureaus have often led to indebted people being allowed to fall into a bottomless pit of borrowing and owing credit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope MAS will also closely scrutinise the people who are appointed to the board of these LCBs so that sensitive information does not fall into the hands of the wrong people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also important that the members of LCBs are not open to all and sundry, and we end up with compromising sensitive information to the wrong people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Enabling consumers to access their credit report whenever they wish to, and to monitor and rectify credit information is a good move.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With increasing incidences of identity theft, this is crucial in helping consumers exercise personal responsibility of their transaction records.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The LCBs' credit monitoring system also sends email notifications when key changes are detected on the credit file.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This means that the consumer can easily detect fraudulent attempts to take credit in his or her name.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On a related note, it is also important for LCBs to have a second authentication system to protect the data.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A data leak is potentially damaging and embarrassing for all users of the system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A credit monitoring system is useful, but one should not be over-reliant on it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are blind spots as the system does not monitor loans from unlicensed credit bureaus, credit lenders, friends, relatives, colleagues and so forth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The "buy now, pay later" concept is not an excuse to live beyond one's means.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Good planning skills and foresight are important to ensure that one does not eventually become enslaved by debt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I take the opportunity to highlight and seek clarification on the following three areas of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the Bill draws a distinction between members and approved members of an LCB.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under section 30(2) of the Bill, an LCB is only permitted to disclose customer information received from any of its members to an approved member.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Section 29(1) and the First Schedule of the Bill contemplate that the following are deemed approved members of the LCB namely, banks, merchant banks, finance companies and credit card issuers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This corresponds to the categories of persons who are authorised to receive customer credit information from credit bureaus under the Third Schedule of the Banking Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under section 29(3) and (4) of the Bill, LCB members who are not deemed approved members have to apply to MAS through the LCB to be approved as approved members of the LCB.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Could the Minister please clarify the circumstances in which approvals will be provided?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the other hand, there has been at least one incident in the past where MAS has approved a licensed moneylender on an ad hoc basis to have access to customer information provided by credit bureaus.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is it therefore contemplated that such entities are at liberty to be approved members of LCB?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, what are MAS' considerations in considering such applications and deciding whether to grant approval to be an approved member of the LCB?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I further note that section 16 of the Bill contemplates that third parties may obtain credit reports with the written consent of the data subject.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will allow parties, such as prospective employers, clubs and associations and so on, to procure credit reports from applicants before considering them for admission.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indeed, I note that the Casino Regulatory Authority of Singapore (CRA) requires applicants for special employee licences under the Casino Control Act to allow the CRA access to the applicant's reports from the credit bureaus.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In many of these instances, the applicant would be providing his written consent out of necessity of the situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He or she would not have any real control over the use of the confidential information provided by the LCB to the third parties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even though, in theory, he may have some options under the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), these are not transactions between equals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For this reason, would the Minister please consider protecting the confidentiality of this information, along similar lines provided for in section 33 of the Bill dealing with the duty of the approved members protecting the confidentiality of customer information obtained from the LCB?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: MLCB is run by DP Information Group, which also operates one of the two LCBs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Having two separate regimes would not serve the purpose of assessing the overall credit worthiness of borrowers and to help borrowers avoid borrowing beyond their means.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also no reason why MLCB and their members should not be subject to the same duties and responsibilities as LCBs and their members relating to customer information and maintaining the security and integrity of data, as set out in Parts 3 and 6 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In these circumstances, may I please ask the reasons for keeping the MLCB regime separate from LCB?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I stress again that the issues of protecting customer information and maintaining the security and integrity of data must surely be as important for MLCB as it is for LCB.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Moving to my third point, I support the objectives of the Bill to protect customer interest by affording customers the right to access, review and rectify their credit records vis-à-vis the LCB and approved members.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Sections 18 and 35 of the Bill allows the customer to request that the LCB and the approved member correct an error of omission in any data that has been processed by the LCB or is in the possession and control of the approved members.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The LCB or approved member has then to conduct and complete an investigation to ascertain the integrity of the data and must correct the data unless it is satisfied on reasonable grounds that a correction should not be made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: MAS further highlighted in its response to feedback from public consultation that LCBs and members should institute appropriate processes to verify the disputed data against relevant documentary information.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Section 23B(4) of the Australian Privacy Act also provides for an escalation mechanism, where an individual dissatisfied with the decision may first complain to the credit reporting body or the credit provider itself and, thereafter, make a further complaint to an external dispute resolution provider, such as the credit ombudsman service or the information commissioner.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While the Bill does not contain similar provisions, I note that section 22 of the PDPA provides for correction of personal data, and section 28 provides for the Personal Data Protection Commissioner to review a refusal to correct data.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I further note that the provisions of the Bill are in addition to the PDPA and the definition of "personal data" in the latter Act is broad enough to include data, as defined in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Globally, most large international markets have moved towards the regulation of credit bureaus.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After the scare of the 2008 Financial Crisis, jurisdictions quickly shifted towards stricter controls to close the loopholes allowing for unethical practices by credit bureaus.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We quickly learnt that these malpractices were a major factor contributing to the crisis, and that governments need to act fast to prevent future crises of this scale.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is timely for Singapore to keep in line with international standards and practices, alongside countries like the US, Japan and Hong Kong, and for us to develop a compatible regulatory regime, especially as international financial markets become increasingly globalised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Domestically, we have also moved towards an era of stronger privacy laws.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The PDPA was a game changer for Singapore, and I am eager that we continue this trend to strengthen consumer rights.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rapidly evolving nature of this market also means that more and more data is being collected, much of it highly sensitive and private information, and much of it unbeknownst to consumers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They were not even aware that free credit reports were available to them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To be honest, I did not know as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As more young borrowers want to gain access to credit, they should be empowered to keep track of what their credit information is saying about their financial health.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am encouraged that section 16 of this Bill addresses this head-on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this light, I strongly agree with the move for MAS to enact formal supervision over credit bureaus, closely monitoring their activities and how they safeguard sensitive data belonging to consumers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Has MAS considered whether new entrants into this industry will benefit Singapore's economy and, if so, can the Minister share their plans to register new credit bureaus?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Without a level-playing field for industry players, like every industry, there will be a lack of innovation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Especially in our rapidly evolving market, where new payment solutions are springing up, credit bureaus also need to be on their feet, seeking out new sources of data, adjusting their analytical tools and algorithms to ensure they provide a holistic view of a person's creditworthiness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would seem that a lack of competition will lead to a lack of incentives to innovate, resulting in an environment where credit bureaus are allowed to be complacent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While Singapore progresses towards the regulation of credit bureaus, I believe that we also need more competition and incentives for innovation to encourage credit bureaus to deliver their service better.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This can also protect customers against credit bureaus for negligent inclusion of inaccurate information, if any, in their credit reports.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Regulating credit bureaus to the standards of developed countries, such as the US and Australia, is, indeed, a timely move.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened to note that MAS conducted public consultations and some of the feedback has been incorporated into the Bill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Subjecting credit bureaus to formal supervision and annual audits by MAS preserves the integrity of the data collected on customers to determine their creditworthiness to facilitate credit assessment and loan decision.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This will also ensure no customers are being evaluated incorrectly on their credit assessment, resulting in adverse outcome for the customers and, in some cases, undue inconvenience, hardship and loss of confidence and reputation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: First, under section 17(3b), that is, "Duty to provide access to data", Licensed Credit Bureaus (LCBs) are required to provide consumers with copies of the credit reports at no cost within 30 days, as specified by the Authority.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Does this refer to a consumer's full credit history?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is there any timeframe involved similar to that of the PDPA requirement on organisations for LCBs to provide consumers' credit information data for the past one year, upon request?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Second, under section 34(1b), that is, "Duty to maintain security and integrity of data and for members to protect any data received from the LCB by making reasonable security arrangements", what is considered "reasonable"?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This can be subjective and may lead to members' own interpretation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is there any guideline or benchmark set for reasonableness?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Third, under section 56, that is, "Authority must cease to be in control of LCB's relevant business when the Authority is satisfied…" What is the recommended maximum timeframe for the Authority to assume control of the LCBs?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be closer monitoring of the affected LCBs that were assumed control of by the Authority?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will the public, that is, customers, be notified that the Authority has assumed control and the reasons for having done so?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will the customers' credit information and credit rating data held by the LCBs be protected and secured during this period?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What assurance can the customers have on all these matters?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, are employers permitted to check on the job applicant's or employee's credit information from the LCB without the consent of the individual?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Do employers fall under the MAS' "approved member list"?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If so, are employers required to comply with the standards of safeguarding this information?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What if the LCB has provided incorrect credit information of that individual which results in the individual not being able to secure the job or, for that matter, banks rejecting a customer's loan application?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can the affected individual or customer seek damages against the LCB for the harm done to his or her reputation and the loss of income as a result of inaccurate information provided?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: To what extent are such inaccuracies prevalent in Singapore's credit bureaus?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are customers able to receive a free copy of their credit report from the credit reporting bureaus once a year?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This will make it easy for customers to identify and dispute inaccurate information.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In the same vein, users of the information for credit, insurance or employment purposes must be responsible for safeguarding the customers' credit information.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Act itself will enable MAS to regulate the consumer and corporate credit reporting business.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The enhanced Act will afford greater confidentiality and security to customers in the protection of their credit information.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have some concerns and suggestions for the consideration of the Minister.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the format is standardised, it will help ensure consistency and minimise confusion among the users.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be a disservice to consumers and businesses if misunderstandings arise due to different presentations and layouts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I understand that formats are usually not hardwired into legislation, credit reports are sensitive documents which can have an important impact on families and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If different credit rating bureaus use different models of assessments, the conclusions of their credit reports for the same client can be very different.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I would like to seek clarification on this aspect.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important to set consistent guidelines on the update of the credit records, including improvement of financial situation or data rectifications, to ensure the clients can access the credit or loans they need in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister in charge of MAS, let me now address their questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To better protect sensitive credit data is one of the key objectives of enacting or introducing this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi asked if MAS can ensure institutions upgrade their data protection security systems.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By formalising MAS' supervision of credit bureaus, the Bill will strengthen data security.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: LCBs and their approved members will now be subject to MAS' technology risk management notices and guidelines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are required to do so now once the Bill becomes law.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These set out MAS' requirements and expectations on the IT controls to protect consumer data from unauthorised access or disclosure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With this new legislation, should there be any gaps in controls, MAS can take the supervisory and enforcement action to get the relevant entity to improve its data security.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And this will have to be an ongoing process even after the Bill becomes law.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Further, membership of licensed credit bureaus will be tightly controlled and subject to MAS' approval.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I actually was not quite aware of the case raised that a licensed moneylender had access to data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the idea is that only entities that have a bona fide need for bank credit information and can safeguard the data security competently, such as banks, merchant banks, finance companies and credit card issuers regulated by MAS, may be admitted as approved members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, in response to Ms Thanaletchimi, employers who wish to screen their employees' credit records must seek their employees' consent to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They cannot just obtain those reports merely by becoming approved members of LCBs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To minimise the risk of data security lapses by the new applicants, MAS will assess any new applicant using the same stringent standards expected of regulated financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if licensed moneylenders apply, they will be subject to the regulations and standards expected of financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some of these criteria will include robust internal controls on system access as well as security.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As Mr Murali Pillai pointed out, an individual may give consent for an LCB to share his credit records with a third party, such as his employer or a country club.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In such cases, the individual will be protected under the PDPA which requires the third party, say, the employer, to comply with the requirements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use and disclosure of the personal data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The safeguards in the Credit Bureau Bill are not applicable because MAS' regulatory ambit would not extend to such third parties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is relying back on the PDPA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second area is on the need for timely, comprehensive and reliable data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat raised the concern that someone who racks up credit card bills is unable to pay and then takes out additional loans to pay them off and then snowballing the debt.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And he wondered if there was a time lag between his near default and his next credit application.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Information at the credit bureaus is updated promptly, monthly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The current rules allow an individual to take unsecured loans such as through credit card bills, up to 24 months of his monthly salary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think that is the issue, and that is why the individual can take a loan to pay off his previous credit card bills because he is allowed up to 24 months.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But just for the record, I am not making an announcement.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Murali Pillai asked if data from the Integrated Resorts (IRs) and licensed moneylenders should also be included in the LCBSs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The answer is yes, if the data is relevant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS and MinLaw are studying and will be announcing measures to allow for more comprehensive credit bureau data in due course.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS will also explore with the Casino Regulatory Authority whether information on the type of credit offered by IRs is relevant to the licensed credit bureaus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once we have the Act, I think we are able to do so more readily.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should clarify that the Bill does not apply to MLCB as it will still be regulated by MinLaw under the Moneylenders Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This approach allows MinLaw to set requirements for members of MLCB that are more suitable for and in line with the existing regulations for moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think it is quite safe to say that MAS does not have some of the expertise to regulate moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Bill also requires LCBs and their approved members to maintain data accuracy and completeness and empowers MAS to take enforcement actions against errant LCBs and their approved members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS will also set more detailed expectations on the timeliness of reporting and data accuracy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, in response to Ms Thanaletchimi, the average data error rates have been very low historically.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There were also a few questions on credit reports.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In response to Ms Thanaletchimi, I would like to highlight that the credit report on the borrower shows his comprehensive payment history over the past one year and any defaults over the past three years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will enable MAS to promote consistent reporting formats by LCBs so as to reduce confusion to consumers and lenders, as suggested by Mr Gan Thiam Poh.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh suggested standardising credit scoring models across all credit bureaus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But as suggested by Mr Louis Ng too, there should also be some competition and a variety of practices which will be conducive to encouraging innovation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we have to strike a balance here.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The credit bureaus each use their own proprietary credit scoring methodologies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To standardise them can unnecessarily stifle research and innovation in developing more accurate ways to predict default.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nonetheless, it is important that credit scoring models must be reliable, whichever model you want to use.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To that end, MAS will supervise LCBs to check that they back test their models against historical data to ensure that the models are predictive and reliable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we will not insist that the methodologies must be the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Ms Thanaletchimi raised a number of consumer protection issues regarding dispute resolution and access to free credit reports.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To better protect consumers, the Bill requires LCBs and their approved members to investigate and rectify data errors on a timely basis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS will set expectations on proper governance arrangements, including for dispute resolution and turnaround times for this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Bill empowers MAS to conduct inspections and investigations and take appropriate enforcement actions against errant LCBs or their approved members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked if consumers could rely on protection under PDPA to correct data errors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To overlapping requirements, PDPA will not apply since the Bill already provides the mechanism for consumers to resolve data errors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will allow the consumer to dispute any data error or engage his lender on a credit decision.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested allowing more credit bureaus to operate to spur innovation in the market.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS also has to strike a balance here between protecting competition against the risk of data fragmentation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The latter would lead to inefficiencies, because the lender would have to approach multiple credit bureaus for their credit reports in order to form a comprehensive view of a borrower's credit history across all lenders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Other markets of similar sizes, such as Hong Kong and Taiwan, have only one consumer credit bureau.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether banks are required to contribute comprehensive data to CBS only and not to DP Credit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is actually no such requirement at all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Banks are free to decide which LCBs they wish to be a member of.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whichever they join, they would contribute data to that credit bureau.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Next, on the governance of LCBs, Mr Saktiandi Supaat raised the need for proper personnel to be appointed to the boards of LCBs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS will require LCBs to assess prospective directors and chief executive officers for their fitness and propriety.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These assessments will include the financial standing and integrity of the relevant individuals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If they are found to be not fit and proper, MAS may remove the directors and chief executive officers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In an extreme case, where the officers and employees of substantial shareholders of an LCB are found to be not fit and proper, MAS may revoke the licence of the credit bureau.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When an LCB faces financial or operational distress, MAS can assume control of the credit bureau to ensure that its credit reporting business continues to operate smoothly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked if such an assumption of control be subject to any time limit and whether the public will be notified.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The objective of MAS assuming control is to restore stable credit reporting operations and avoid any disruption to consumers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is difficult to estimate upfront how long this will take because it will depend on various factors, including the cost of the financial and operation requests.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But please be reassured that it is not in the interest of MAS to assume control longer than necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our priority is always to put the entity back on a firm footing to restore confidence in the operation of the credit reporting system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And MAS will make public any assumption of control of an LCB via a Government Gazette.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am confident that with the Bill, we will strengthen Singapore's credit reporting industry so that borrowers and lenders can better manage their finances and risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But at the same time, MAS has introduced a range of measures over the past few years to promote prudent lending and borrowing behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This covers diverse products, from property loans to motor vehicle loans and unsecured credit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, we are ultimately responsible for our own financial well-being.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With that, Madam, I beg to move.      .
